synopsis: The braking system must work in rain, snow, fog, dust, dusk, darkness and glare, but the mid-2027 validation window will not include snow and cold conditions [f285, f2033, f3676, f8255, f4403]. Dust is identified as the biggest off-road sensor-simulation gap, and perception models for dust, rain, mud and occlusion are the hardest technical gap in virtual validation; construction and mining studies from 2023–2026 report lidar degradation in real dust [f89, f10338, f6688]. Lidar rain-and-fog simulation is the best-validated case, based on on-road evidence, but agreement depends on matching real conditions and deteriorates as fog visibility falls [f4412, f7556, f7557, f7558]. A fog-chamber test found that at 10 m visibility all lidars but one failed to detect a target at 10.5 m; if dust prevents person detection at the required stopping range, speed must decrease or stopping cannot be promised [f7559, f11330]. Snow, glare and darkness validation remains weak or absent, while raw sensor-log replay does not retest contamination, vibration or glare upstream of the re-injection point and cannot establish performance in environmental conditions absent from the logs [f6488, f96, f5241]. Incident evidence does not establish adverse weather's share of collisions, and published complete-system off-road false-positive and false-negative rates were not found; planning therefore must allocate environmental variability to simulation, uncertainty bounds or residual physical testing, with adverse-environment sensor models experimentally correlated [f3234, f3235, f6385, f10348, f5219].
